fields.title: Chatbot to Agent Progression
fields.summary: Three Python scripts that step from a stateless single-turn chatbot to a tool-using agent, using LangChain and Claude — a teaching artifact that makes the progression explicit.
fields.business_problem: "Chatbot" and "AI agent" get used interchangeably, but they're not the same thing. New engineers (and non-engineers asking for AI features) need to see the difference at the code level: where memory lives, when tools enter, and what changes in the loop.
fields.tools_used: Python, LangChain, Anthropic Claude API, DuckDuckGo search
fields.key_features:
- chatbot1.py — stateless single-turn chatbot, every prompt independent
- chatbot2.py — multi-turn with conversation history so the model can refer back
- chatbot3.py — full agent loop: reason → act → observe → repeat, with llm.bind_tools() letting Claude decide when to call DuckDuckGo
- Three message roles for tool use: HumanMessage, AIMessage, ToolMessage
- Handles Claude's two response formats (plain string vs. structured content blocks)
- Sliding-window memory management (system prompt + last 20 messages) to bound the context window
fields.role_contribution: Sole author — wrote all three scripts as MSIS coursework at Baylor University.
fields.biggest_challenge: Implementing the agent loop in chatbot3.py correctly — handling multiple tool calls in one response, threading ToolMessage results back into history, and trimming the window without losing the system prompt.
fields.what_learned: "Memory" and "tools" are the two axes that turn a chatbot into an agent. Both are easy to get wrong: memory grows unbounded if you don't trim; tools cause infinite loops if you don't terminate on a non-tool response.

fields.title: n8n Multi-Agent Booking Pipeline
fields.summary: A multi-agent handyman booking pipeline in n8n — Gemini parses the customer message, deterministic logic prices and schedules, Gemini writes a friendly confirmation, all chained through an orchestrator.
fields.business_problem: A handyman receives free-form messages like "my faucet is leaking, I'm at 1234 Main St, free Thu or Sat". Manually classifying the job, looking up the price, picking slots, and writing a confirmation eats 5+ minutes per lead. The pipeline returns a structured job, estimate, proposed slots, and a confirmation message in seconds.
fields.tools_used: n8n, Google Gemini 2.5 Flash, JSON, HTTP webhooks
fields.key_features:
- 5 workflows: orchestrator, intake-agent (AI), Agent-Pricing (logic), agent-scheduling (logic), agent-comms (AI)
- AI where it earns its keep (extracting service/zip/urgency/preferred_days from a free-form message; writing a ≤120-word confirmation), deterministic logic where it doesn't (pricing, slot filtering)
- Orchestrator chains the four agents over HTTP and stores intermediate state, assembling one final JSON response
- Pricing rules: USD catalog ($120–$160), ZIP-based travel fee ($0/$10/$20), +20% urgency surcharge
- Scheduling: filter 5 hard-coded slots by preferred_days, return up to 3
- Single webhook entry: curl -X POST .../webhook/orchestrator returns the full booking proposal
fields.role_contribution: Sole author — designed the pipeline split, wrote each n8n workflow, defined the JSON contract between agents, and tuned the Gemini prompts for both intake and comms.
fields.biggest_challenge: Deciding what not to do with AI. Pricing and scheduling were originally a single Gemini call until I realized that "compute a number from a table" is exactly what an LLM is bad at. Splitting them out made the pipeline cheaper, faster, and predictable.
fields.what_learned: Agent pipelines win when you treat AI as one tool in a toolbox, not the whole toolbox. The orchestrator + JSON contract pattern lets you swap any single agent (e.g., Gemini → Claude) without touching the others.

fields.title: Handyman AI Assistant
fields.summary: Conversational LangChain agent that quotes handyman jobs, finds calendar availability, and books appointments through natural language.
fields.business_problem: Solo handymen lose hours bouncing between phone calls, a pricing spreadsheet, and Google Calendar to quote jobs and schedule them. Customers want instant answers, not a callback at 9am.
fields.tools_used: Python, LangChain, Google Gemini (gemini-2.5-flash), Google Sheets API, Google Calendar API, OAuth 2.0
fields.key_features:
- Pricing tool reads a Google Sheets price list and uses Gemini to produce a structured quote (price, urgency, complexity)
- Scheduling tool queries Calendar freebusy.query for open slots in morning/afternoon/evening windows
- Booking tool creates a Calendar event only after explicit customer confirmation
- Multi-turn conversational memory via LangChain
- Hardcoded America/Chicago timezone (single-region service)
fields.role_contribution: Sole developer — designed the agent loop, implemented the three tools, set up dual Google auth (service-account for Sheets, OAuth desktop client for Calendar).
fields.biggest_challenge: Keeping the agent from auto-booking before the customer confirmed a slot, plus handling Calendar's freebusy time-zone semantics correctly.
fields.what_learned: Agent quality lives in tool contracts — tight, typed, and idempotent inputs/outputs. Mutating tools (like calendar booking) need an explicit confirmation step in the prompt, not just trust.

fields.title: Machine Learning Exercises (scikit-learn)
fields.summary: A collection of standalone scikit-learn exercises from the Baylor AI course covering KNN classification and linear regression on five classic datasets, with end-to-end EDA, training, and result visualization.
fields.business_problem: Coursework artifact — the goal was hands-on fluency with the scikit-learn pipeline, not solving a single business problem. Each exercise stands on its own as a worked example a student or hiring manager can read in a sitting.
fields.tools_used: Python, scikit-learn, pandas, matplotlib, seaborn, HuggingFace datasets
fields.key_features:
- ml1.py — KNN on load_digits: train/test split → score → confusion-matrix heatmap (seaborn)
- iris.py / iris_claude.py — KNN on iris with label-to-species mapping and per-error inspection
- ml2.py — Linear regression on California Housing: pandas EDA, per-feature scatter plots, coefficients, expected-vs-predicted with a y=x reference line
- ml3.py — Auto MPG: single-feature (weight only) regression saved to PNG, then multi-feature model with 6 predictors
- diabetes.py — Linear regression scatterplot + regression line on the diabetes dataset
- All scripts independent — `python ml1.py` runs a complete pipeline end-to-end
fields.role_contribution: Sole author — wrote every script as classwork at Baylor.
fields.biggest_challenge: Building intuition for why each step matters (train/test split, feature scaling, residual plots) instead of just calling sklearn methods because the lecture said so. The visualizations were the forcing function.
fields.what_learned: sklearn's API is small and consistent (fit / predict / score), but knowing what to show — confusion matrix vs. expected-vs-predicted vs. residuals — is the part that takes practice. A good plot makes a missed class or an outlier obvious in one glance.

fields.title: Campus SkillSwap 1
fields.summary: Student-to-student skill marketplace built spec-first with GitHub Spec Kit — pure Django 5 monolith with server-rendered templates.
fields.business_problem: Students want peer learning (tutoring, design, music) without paid platforms; the team needed a small but real product to test a spec-first AI development workflow.
fields.tools_used: Python, Django 5.2 LTS, SQLite, server-rendered templates, Bootstrap 5, GitHub Spec Kit
fields.key_features:
- 6 user stories authored as specs before any code (specs/001-campus-skillswap/)
- Auth (register, sign in, post a skill)
- Browse + search by case-insensitive title and category
- Booking lifecycle: request → owner accepts / declines
- Star-rating reviews (one per user per skill, replace-in-place)
- Owner-only edit/delete with 403 for non-owners
- Invariants enforced at form (clean()), view, and DB (CheckConstraint / UniqueConstraint)
fields.role_contribution: Sole developer — authored the spec, data model, and tasks before writing code; implemented all 6 user stories to match.
fields.biggest_challenge: Keeping invariants consistent across three layers (form, view, DB) without duplicating logic.
fields.what_learned: Spec-first AI development produces tighter code than free-form prompting; the spec catches edge cases the code would have shipped silently.

fields.title: Campus SkillSwap 2
fields.summary: Same Campus SkillSwap product re-implemented with Claude Code's research-plan-implement methodology on a Django REST + Next.js stack.
fields.business_problem: After building v1 spec-first, I rebuilt the same product on a separate stack to compare AI-driven development methodologies and architectures.
fields.tools_used: Django 5, Django REST Framework, Next.js 16 (App Router), Tailwind v4, React Hook Form, Zod, Cloudinary, PostgreSQL, Render, Claude Code
fields.key_features:
- Two-service architecture: DRF API + Next.js frontend with credentials: include session cookies
- Debounced search with shareable, bookmarkable URL state
- Image upload via Cloudinary (falls back to local disk in dev)
- Toast notifications via sonner
- One-click Render Blueprint deploy via render.yaml
- 15 e2e scenarios (e2e/scenarios.md) all passing
fields.role_contribution: Sole developer — designed the API, built the Next.js client, deployed both services to Render.
fields.biggest_challenge: Keeping session-cookie auth working across localhost:8000 (API) and localhost:3000 (Next.js) in dev, then translating that to the Render two-service deploy.
fields.what_learned: Research-plan-implement loops produce great per-file code but require disciplined re-planning when crossing service boundaries; without that, the API and frontend drift.
